hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=3\sqrt{2-x}$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

Let's write $y=3\sqrt{2-x}$ as $y=3\sqrt{-(x-2)}$ so that it is easier to see the transformations from the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=3\sqrt{2-x}$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt{x}\\\\
f(x-2)&=\sqrt{x-2}\\\\
f(-(x-2))&=\sqrt{-(x-2)}\\\\
3f(-(x-2))&=3\sqrt{-(x-2)}\\\\
&=3\sqrt{2-x}
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=3f(-(x-2))$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x-2$ shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ to the right $2$ units.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A square root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, zero) and passes through (four, two). The shifted function has an endpoint (two, zero) and passes through (six, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $x-2$ by $-1$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-2}$ over the line $x=2$.



[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A square root function graph and its horizontally reflected graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (two, zero) and passes through (six, two). The horizontally reflected graph has an endpoint (two, zero) and passes through (negative two, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $\sqrt{-(x-2)}$ by $3$ stretches the graph of $y=\sqrt{-(x-2)} $ vertically by a factor of $3$.  



[[☃ image 1]]

Note that the graph of the function passes through $(-2,2)$ *before* the stretch, and $(-2, 6 )$ *after* the stretch.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $3$.  

Additionally it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 2]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, two) and passes through (ten, negative one).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/838d19b306cd3a25ac6c67be671bb6a26eaf0e71)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/76bbee52d28bfb5f5bcd72a6831a797eaab9824d)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

options.alt: A square root function graph and its vertically stretched graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (two, zero) and passes through (six, two). The vertically stretched graph has an endpoint (two, zero) and passes through (negative two, six).
